Mortgage prepayment or liquid savings? Compare debt, cash and the same monthly budget

Four graphics reconcile a permitted lump-sum prepayment with keeping the same cash in savings, including unused payments after a mortgage is cleared.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a lump-sum prepayment versus liquid savings

Interactive planning lab

Cash actually applied to mortgage at the start$20,000
Mortgage interest avoided over selected years$4,984.07
Prepay minus keep-cash net financial position$2,902.45

Hypothetical penalty-free permitted lump sum applied at time zero. Mortgage rate is nominal annual compounded semi-annually, converted to a monthly rate, and held fixed through the selected horizon. Both choices retain the original monthly payment computed before prepayment. Savings earn the entered constant effective annual return after tax/costs, converted monthly. Each month savings earn interest, mortgage payments occur, and any unused part of the identical payment budget is deposited into savings. Prepayment is capped at debt; excess starting cash stays liquid. Home value is identical and excluded. No prepayment charge, actual privilege, mortgage interest deduction, renewal, account restriction or investment risk distribution is calculated.

The central idea

Interest avoided is only one part of the comparison. Track accessible savings and debt separately, and keep the monthly payment allocation identical in both choices.

01

Confirm the prepayment terms before comparing the arithmetic

The FCAC’s prepayment guide explains that a mortgage may permit extra payments or lump sums, with limits set by the contract. Paying more than the permitted amount can create a charge. The related rights page describes prepayment disclosures for federally regulated lenders.

This comparison assumes the selected lump sum is permitted without a penalty. It does not calculate a privilege or verify a particular mortgage. A real prepayment charge, access restriction or change in contract terms would need to be added to the decision.

Both choices start with the same mortgage and cash. One applies a lump sum immediately; the other retains that cash in savings. The original monthly mortgage payment is preserved in both, rather than automatically lowered after the prepayment.

02

Match the starting resources and the monthly allocation

The default mortgage is CAD 300,000, with twenty-five years of remaining amortization and a 4.5% quoted nominal annual rate. The example chooses semi-annual compounding converted to an equivalent monthly rate. It produces a scheduled payment of approximately CAD 1,660.42 a month.

A CAD 20,000 prepayment reduces the initial mortgage to CAD 280,000 and leaves none of that selected cash liquid. Keeping the cash leaves the initial debt at CAD 300,000 and the CAD 20,000 available in savings. Home value is identical in both choices and is excluded from the comparison.

Rates remain constant throughout the selected five-year horizon. The model does not predict renewal terms or assume every mortgage follows its chosen compounding convention. Use the actual disclosed calculation and payment schedule for a real contract.

03

Read the cash path beside the mortgage path

With the same scheduled payment applied to less opening debt, the prepayment path has a smaller mortgage throughout the default period. After five years, debt is approximately CAD 238,405.09 with prepayment and CAD 263,389.16 while keeping the cash.

Under the selected 2% effective annual savings return after tax and costs, the retained CAD 20,000 grows to CAD 22,081.62. The prepayment choice has no liquid savings from that sum during the default horizon. The cash chart makes this difference visible instead of counting lower debt as cash on demand.

If a modeled mortgage is cleared before the horizon, the unused part of its original monthly payment allocation moves into savings at month-end. The other choice receives the same treatment. This prevents the comparison from silently spending freed payments in one case while saving them in the other.

04

Reconcile interest avoided with the savings-growth difference

Net financial position in this limited comparison is liquid savings minus mortgage debt. The common home value cancels. Both options begin with the same net position and receive identical monthly payment allocations, so the difference can be reconciled through financing costs and savings growth.

The default prepayment avoids approximately CAD 4,984.07 of mortgage interest over five years. It also gives up CAD 2,081.62 of modeled savings growth. The difference is approximately CAD 2,902.45 in favour of prepayment under these constant assumptions.

The waterfall shows that reconciliation. It is an end-of-horizon nominal comparison, not an annual return, a present-value calculation or a valuation of liquidity. Positive arithmetic does not establish that allocating the selected cash to a mortgage fits the household’s other commitments.

05

Test savings returns and cash amounts without losing the funding match

The matrix supplies alternative initial cash amounts and after-tax savings returns. Each pair keeps the same mortgage, scheduled payment and horizon. Its signed cells show the prepayment choice’s cash-minus-debt position relative to keeping that cell’s cash liquid.

Prepayment cannot exceed the debt in the model. If more cash is entered, the excess remains in savings, and any payment allocation no longer needed for debt also goes there. A zero mortgage or zero selected cash produces no advantage from a prepayment that does not occur.

The savings return is a hypothetical constant net rate, with no investment-risk distribution. The model excludes charges, mortgage-interest deductions, actual account rules and future rate changes. Review the cash reserve needed for other purposes alongside the arithmetic, using confirmed contract terms and a budget that leaves each dollar assigned once.
